services.body_html:
Integrated Logistics Consultancy for Warehouse Operations

United Integrated Logistics provides a broad range of consultancy services covering every aspect of warehouse operations. These services are delivered by a team of professional experts with deep experience in diagnosing problems and designing solutions.

Our remit is to address the challenges you face, whether they concern rising costs, declining efficiency, or the need for a fundamental step change in performance.

Our areas of consultancy expertise

  • Resolving warehouse management challenges: analysing operational bottlenecks and delivering effective solutions.
  • Reducing warehouse operating costs: identifying sources of waste and applying strategies that bring operating costs down.
  • Raising operational efficiency: re-engineering procedures to increase productivity, reduce errors and shorten cycle times.
  • Warehouse layout and organisation: the best arrangement for your warehouse to ensure optimal use of space and smooth flow.
  • Inventory counting consultancy: complete plans and procedures for an accurate, successful count across all periodic and annual stocktakes.
  • Developing warehouse staff skills: designing and delivering specialist training programmes that raise team capability.
  • Getting the most from your WMS: maximising the value of your current warehouse management system, or helping you select a new one.
  • Equipment and tooling selection: impartial technical advice on choosing and purchasing the right equipment at high efficiency and a sensible price.

From advice to implementation oversight

Our services do not stop at the consultancy report. At the client's request, the United Integrated team can take direct charge of supervising the implementation of the recommendations, ensuring the solutions are applied correctly on the ground and deliver the intended results.

services.title: Inventory Counting and Fixed Asset Registration
services.short: An independent, impartial third party for counting goods and inventory, with the accuracy to expose errors before they turn into financial losses.
services.seo_title: Inventory Counting & Stocktaking Services Saudi Arabia
services.seo_desc: Independent third-party stocktaking and fixed-asset counting: annual wall-to-wall, cycle counts and spot audits, with audit-ready discrepancy reports.
services.body_html:
Professional accuracy that makes your financial and operational data reliable

Inventory accuracy underpins the financial and operational performance of any business. Gaps between physical and book balances translate directly into financial losses, poor purchasing decisions and delays in fulfilling customer orders.

United Integrated Logistics provides a complete professional service as an independent, impartial third party for counting goods and inventory. We deliver an accurate, structured and fast count that exposes operational errors before they turn into financial losses, protects you against waste and theft, and gives you reliable data to support your strategic decisions.

"Don't let stock disappear between the numbers." With us, counting is not a burden — it is a strategic tool for your success.

Our methodology for managing and executing counts

1. Planning and preparation (before the count)

  • Preparing the working environment: clear operational guidance for setting up the warehouse and readying goods for a clean count.
  • Zoning: dividing the warehouse into intelligent count zones based on the volume, nature and classification of items.
  • Mapping movement routes: defining the counting method, assigning responsibilities and setting a strict movement plan that guarantees full coverage.

2. Execution and on-site supervision (during the count)

  • Direct oversight: United Integrated supervisors monitor the counting teams on site in real time.
  • Tagging: marking goods once counted to guarantee full coverage and prevent double counting.
  • Immediate resolution: spotting, reporting and resolving any deviations or obstacles on the spot, without disrupting operations.

3. Reporting and intelligent analysis (after the count)

  • Final reconciliation: detailed, classified final listings of every item counted.
  • Inventory Discrepancy Report: a precise report setting out the gaps between physical and book balances.
  • Advisory recommendations: recommendations and solutions to strengthen inventory controls and raise operational efficiency going forward.

The types of count we cover

Annual Wall-to-Wall Inventory

Our most requested service, timed with the financial year end and a mandatory step in closing the accounts, with a direct impact on the financial statements. It involves freezing stock movement (where possible) and counting every item "wall to wall" with exacting accuracy, with an immediate recount of any item showing a variance.

Cycle Counting

Keeps inventory data accurate throughout the year without halting your daily operations. We count selected items — at random or by ABC classification — on a daily, weekly or monthly cycle, concentrating on high-value or fast-moving goods.

Spot and Surprise Audits

A rigorous control tool carried out without prior notice to warehouse staff, verifying the balances of specific items and acting as a strong deterrent against theft, waste and internal manipulation.

Fixed asset counting and registration

Counting and tagging fixed assets, reconciling them against the accounting asset register, and issuing a report on variances and on any missing or unregistered assets.

What counting services with United Integrated deliver

  • Verified inventory: certainty that physical quantities match the book records.
  • Approved, reliable reports: an impartial audit reference for internal and external auditors.
  • Early detection of operational errors: identifying storage and recording errors and inconsistencies in goods received and issued.
  • Tighter control and integrity: reducing the risk of malpractice, manipulation and internal theft.
  • Lower cost and effort: freeing up your resources to focus on your core business by relying on our specialist team.
  • Stronger strategic decisions: greater confidence in buying, selling and production planning.

services.title: Warehouse Operations Improvement and Development
services.short: In-depth analysis that turns your warehouse from a cost centre into a core driver of business success, with cost reductions of up to 20%.
services.seo_desc: Improve inbound, storage, picking and despatch with a four-stage methodology and warehouse KPIs that cut operating costs and raise productivity.
services.body_html:
From cost centre to growth engine

Every warehouse faces its own challenges, but the objective is the same: lower operating costs and higher operational efficiency. Picking errors, delays at goods-in and poor use of space all eat into your margin. At United Integrated we do not offer off-the-shelf fixes; we deliver a deep, comprehensive analysis that turns your warehouse into a core driver of business success.

Our four-stage methodology

  • Assess: a deep analysis of current operations, identifying weak points and sources of waste.
  • Design: solutions and procedures built specifically for your business to raise efficiency and cut cost.
  • Implement: working alongside you to apply the improvements and train your team on them.
  • Monitor: using key performance indicators (KPIs) to ensure the results are sustained.

The four elements of a successful warehouse operation

  • The system (WMS): how effectively your system supports day-to-day operations.
  • The workforce: the capability, productivity and training of your staff.
  • Policies and procedures: the clarity of the standard operating procedures (SOPs) in use.
  • Layout and planning: how effective the internal layout of the warehouse is.

A full analysis of every warehouse process

1. Improving inbound operations

Correct receiving is the foundation of accurate inventory. We review and improve:

  • How documents (purchase order, invoice) are checked and matched.
  • The speed and accuracy of unloading and sorting goods.
  • Recording variances and mismatches and reporting them immediately.
  • Updating the WMS with received quantities in real time.
  • Moving goods and directing them to the correct storage locations.

2. Improving storage and stock keeping

  • Optimal use of space and reduction of wasted area.
  • Effective application of first in, first out (FIFO).
  • Storing goods safely and correctly, in line with handling instructions.
  • Easy access to goods at the pick face to speed up order preparation.

3. Improving outbound and order preparation

  • Sending the right goods, in the right quantity, to the right customer.
  • Reducing order cycle time from receipt through to despatch.
  • Retaining and properly archiving proofs of delivery (PODs).
  • A clear mechanism for handling and managing customer returns and rejections.

Beyond process: performance and data

Putting key performance indicators (KPIs) in place

You cannot improve what you cannot measure. We help you define and apply the right indicators for your warehouse, such as:

  • Inventory accuracy.
  • Operating cost per square metre.
  • Inventory turnover rate.
  • Average order preparation time.

Staff performance and training

Your people are your most valuable asset. We assess performance on productivity, collaboration and commitment, and deliver on-the-job training that raises team capability and keeps the improvements in place after the project ends.

Warehouse Operations and Management Services (4PL)

Raising the performance of your existing team under expert leadership

Our approach to warehouse supervision

services.title: Logistics Audit of Warehouse Operations
services.short: An impartial technical report exposing weak areas, bottlenecks and sources of waste in your operating cycle.
services.seo_desc: In-depth logistics audit of warehouse operations: core processes, inventory control, reporting, safety and security, resource efficiency and SOPs.
services.body_html:
Logistics Audit for Warehouse Operations

United Integrated Logistics provides a professional logistics audit service, giving your management an in-depth technical report on the efficiency of operations in your warehouses. The core objective is to pinpoint weak areas, identify where you are exposed to risk, and capture every available opportunity for improvement.

What the logistics audit covers

  • Core processes: analysis of goods receiving, storage, despatch and distribution procedures.
  • Inventory control: assessment of counting accuracy and of stock control and monitoring mechanisms.
  • Reporting and communication: review of the reporting system (dead stock, slow movers, obsolescence) and of the channels used to communicate with other departments.
  • Safety and security: review of the procedures protecting stock and people in the warehouse.
  • Resource efficiency: measuring how well the available resources — space, equipment and staff — are being used.
  • Systems and SOPs: auditing approved systems and regulations and the degree of compliance with them.

The objective: pinpointing shortfalls and bottlenecks

By assessing the warehouse operation as a whole, we give you a clear, impartial report identifying shortfalls, bottlenecks and sources of waste in your operating cycle.

An important note on scope

This service is purely diagnostic; the final report focuses on identifying and describing problems and shortfalls, without proposing solutions within its scope. If the client wants an action plan and implementation proposals, we move to the warehouse operations improvement and development service, which is the next step on from this one.

services.title: Storage Location Coding and Numbering
services.short: From designing the coding system through to printing and fixing the labels — the first step to a successful WMS.
services.seo_desc: Warehouse location coding and numbering: coding system design, high-quality barcode label printing and precise on-site installation inside the warehouse.
services.body_html:
The foundation of an efficient warehouse: knowing where every item sits

United Integrated Logistics provides a complete service for coding and numbering storage locations, from design through to installation. We help you determine the best coding system for your warehouse, based on the nature of the materials stored and the type of storage in use — floor, shelving or racking.

Our approach to warehouse location coding

1. Consultation and system design

Our expert team works with the client on the design and naming of storage locations, taking account of label size and material with a focus on durability, longevity and cost, so the solution lasts and suits the warehouse environment.

2. Label design and printing

Once the proposed design is approved, we design and print the location labels — barcode or numeric — to the highest quality.

3. Precise installation and fixing

Our technical team installs and fixes the printed labels in their correct positions inside the warehouse, so the system is applied in full.

The result: faster, more accurate access to goods

The service directly accelerates handling operations, increases location accuracy and makes it easier for staff to reach goods on demand. This level of organisation is the first step towards implementing any warehouse management system (WMS) successfully.

services.title: Warehouse Organisation, Layout and Relocation
services.short: We are not a furniture removals company — we are warehouse relocation specialists, working to a logistics methodology that protects your stock.
services.seo_desc: Warehouse organisation using ABC classification, plus complete site-to-site relocation that protects stock integrity and arranges it at the new location.
services.body_html:
Part one: warehouse organisation and layout (internal improvement)

Organising products well inside the warehouse directly raises operational efficiency: it shortens the time taken to pick or receive goods, lowers the error rate and improves accuracy across every process. When organising and arranging the warehouse, our team takes account of:

  • The nature of the products: designing the storage system — floor, shelving or racking — around the materials being stored.
  • Aisle design and equipment: setting the right aisle width for the handling equipment in use.
  • ABC analysis: storing fast-moving goods in easily accessible locations.
  • Slow-moving and dead stock: allocating upper or rear areas to slow-moving materials.
  • Securing assets: keeping high-value goods in secure, locked locations accessible only to named personnel.

Part two: warehouse relocation and transfer (a complete move)

Moving an entire warehouse from one site to another is a complex, sensitive logistics operation that demands more than simply "moving" — it demands the expertise to protect stock integrity and keep the business running.

We are not a furniture removals company. We are warehouse relocation specialists — and unlike removals firms, we understand the value of inventory and approach the move with a logistics methodology that ensures no goods are damaged or lost in transit.

  • Stock integrity: complete preservation of the quantity and quality of the goods moved.
  • Organisation at the new site: goods arranged professionally and methodically at the new location from day one.
  • Strategic planning: accounting for the nature of the goods, how often they are requested and their volume, so every item is easy to reach the moment operations restart.

posts.title: Why Your Stocktake Belongs in Independent Hands
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: When a warehouse team counts its own stock, it is auditing its own work. Here is why auditors insist on an independent party — and what actually changes in the numbers.
posts.body:
The structural flaw in counting your own stock

When a warehouse team counts its own inventory, a problem arises that has less to do with integrity than with how the work is structured: the team is reviewing the results of its own performance. And an eye accustomed to a place stops seeing the faults in it.

Layered on top of this is an unspoken pressure: the count result is read as an assessment of the team itself, which creates a tendency — conscious or otherwise — to explain variances away rather than record them.

Three things an independent party changes

1. Neutrality in recording

An independent team has no stake in the outcome of the count. It records what it sees, not what it is expected to see. That alone is enough to produce a tangible shift in the accuracy of the figures.

2. Credibility with auditors

A stocktaking report issued by an independent external party carries weight as audit evidence with internal and external reviewers alike, sparing the finance function a long argument at year-end close.

3. Rapid mobilisation without disruption

An in-house count means pulling your own staff off their core duties for days. An external team arrives with sufficient headcount and a ready plan, and executes within a tight window. The saving here is not in the cost of counting, but in the cost of downtime.

And what about the cost difference?

The sharper question is not "what does an external stocktake cost?" but "what does it cost me not to know my true stock position?" Once you account for unnecessary purchasing, dead stock and late orders, an independent count often moves from the expense column to the savings column.
posts.seo_title: Third-Party Stocktaking: Why Auditors Require It
posts.seo_desc: Why inventory counting belongs with an independent third party: neutral recording, audit credibility and fast mobilisation without disrupting operations.

posts.title: ABC Analysis: The Simplest Way to Re-Sequence Your Warehouse
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: Twenty per cent of your SKUs account for eighty per cent of your movement. ABC analysis is how that rule of thumb turns into concrete decisions about storage locations and counting schedules.
posts.body:
From the Pareto principle to the warehouse floor

In most warehouses, a small proportion of items accounts for the largest share of movement and value. ABC analysis translates that observation into three practical categories, each handled differently.

How do you classify?

Class A: high-value or fast-moving items — few in number, large in impact.
Class B: moderate in value and movement.
Class C: low-value or slow-moving items — many in number, limited in impact.

Classification can be based on item value, on movement rate, or on a combination of the two. The choice is not a detail: value-based classification serves financial control, while movement-based classification serves operational efficiency.

Three decisions the classification changes immediately

1. Storage locations

Class A items go in the locations closest to the dispatch area and at easy-reach height (the golden zone). Class C items move to upper or rear zones. This change alone measurably reduces the daily walking distance of the picking team.

2. Counting frequency

There is no sense in counting every item at the same frequency. Class A is counted monthly, B quarterly, C annually. The result: higher accuracy for less effort.

3. Reorder levels

Class A items warrant close monitoring and carefully calculated safety stock. Class C items are managed with simpler levels, without burdening management with daily tracking of low-impact lines.

A common mistake

Classification is not a one-off exercise. Item movement shifts seasonally and year on year, and a Class A item this year may become a C next year. Review the classification at least twice a year.
posts.seo_title: ABC Analysis in Warehouses: Layout and Counting
posts.seo_desc: A practical guide to ABC analysis: how to classify your items, and how it reshapes storage locations, cycle counting frequency and reorder levels.

posts.title: FIFO and FEFO: Why the Rule Is Clear but the Practice Fails
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: Every warehouse knows "first in, first out". Yet damaged and expired stock turns up in almost every count. The problem is not the rule — it is the design.
posts.body:
The rule is well known; the practice is rare

There is no warehouse that does not know the FIFO principle (first in, first out), and no pharmaceutical or food warehouse that does not know FEFO (first expired, first out). Yet damaged and expired stock appears in every count. Why?

Reason one: the design works against the rule

When new goods are stored in front of older ones in the same location, you are asking the operative to make an extra effort in order to follow the rule. And a rule that demands extra effort is not followed consistently.

The fix is a design fix, not a training one: storage locations that allow loading from one side and picking from the opposite side, or separate locations allocated to different batches.

Reason two: no batch traceability

If the system knows only the quantity, with no receipt date or batch number, there is no way to tell which units are older. Batch/lot tracking is not a luxury in shelf-life sectors — it is a basic requirement.

Reason three: no measure

What is not measured is not done. Measure the proportion of items picked in the correct sequence, and the ratio of damaged stock to total inventory, monthly. When the figure appears in a report that gets discussed, behaviour changes.

When do you choose FEFO over FIFO?

With shelf-life goods, the oldest receipt is not necessarily the nearest expiry. Pharmaceuticals, food and chemicals are always managed under FEFO — and confusing the two carries a direct cost in write-offs.
posts.seo_title: FIFO and FEFO in Warehouses: Why They Fail
posts.seo_desc: Why FIFO and FEFO fail in practice despite clear rules: layouts that fight the rule, missing batch traceability and absent KPIs — plus how to fix each one.

posts.title: Before You Buy a WMS: Five Questions That Settle the Decision
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: Many WMS projects fail not because the system is poor, but because the warehouse was not ready for it. These five questions expose your readiness before you sign the contract.
posts.body:
A system does not fix what is broken

The most common thing we see in warehouse management system implementations is a mistaken expectation: that the system will solve problems of operational discipline. In reality, a system documents existing practice more precisely — so if that practice is wrong, it documents the error faithfully.

1. Are your storage locations coded and numbered?

A system works on the logic of "item in location". Without clear, fixed location coding, there is nothing tying the system to reality. This is step zero — and ignoring it is the most common cause of stalled projects.

2. Are your procedures documented (SOPs)?

Implementing a system requires defining who does what and when. If procedures are not documented before the project, they will be written in haste during it — and they will reflect the disorder rather than remedy it.

3. How accurate is your inventory today?

Migrating inaccurate data into a new system produces an inaccurate system. Start with a wall-to-wall inventory that establishes the baseline, then migrate.

4. Who will own the system once the project ends?

Every system needs an internal owner who understands it and develops its use. Without that role, the system will only ever be used as far as staff were trained in the first week, and then it freezes.

5. Do you genuinely need a new system?

In more cases than you might think, the current system is capable of far more than is being used. Before buying a new one, examine whether the problem lies in the tool or in how it is used — the difference between the two is hundreds of thousands of riyals.
posts.seo_title: Choosing a WMS: Five Questions Before You Buy
posts.seo_desc: Before buying a WMS: are your locations coded? Are your SOPs documented? How accurate is your inventory? Who owns the system? And do you really need it?

posts.title: SOPs: The Line Between a Warehouse That Runs and One That Depends on People
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: If one absent employee throws your warehouse into disarray, you do not have a system — you have people. Standard operating procedures are what turn individual experience into an institutional asset.
posts.body:
A simple test

Ask yourself: if your warehouse supervisor were away for a week, how much work would grind to a halt? If the answer is "a great deal", then the knowledge in your warehouse is stored in people's heads rather than in the way the operation works.

What are standard operating procedures, really?

They are not a file in a manager's drawer. They are a written, concise description of every recurring process: who performs it, through which steps, with which document, and what counts as completing it correctly.

The minimum you must have

  • Receiving procedure: document matching, inspection, recording, and handling of variances.
  • Put-away procedure: rules for selecting a location and updating the system.
  • Picking and dispatch procedure: verification before shipping and documentation of handover.
  • Returns procedure: inspection, classification, and either return to stock or disposal.
  • Cycle counting procedure: scope, frequency, and the mechanism for handling variances.

Why do written procedures fail?

For two recurring reasons: they are written in management language that the people carrying out the work do not read, and they are not tied to any follow-up. A procedure whose compliance is never reviewed becomes, within months, a historical document.

Start small

Do not try to document everything at once. Pick the process where errors recur most, document it on a single page, train people on it, and measure the effect for a month. Then move on to the next.
posts.seo_title: Warehouse SOPs: A Practical Implementation Guide

posts.title: Warehouse Shrinkage: Where Your Stock Actually Leaks Away
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: Shrinkage is usually filed under a single word: theft. Our field experience says the larger share is operational error — and simple controls close most of it.
posts.body:
Shrinkage Is Not a Synonym for Theft

When a stocktake throws up a negative variance, the mind jumps straight to theft. In most cases, however, shrinkage is a composite of several sources, and theft is only one of them — and usually not the largest.

The Five Most Common Sources

1. Receiving Errors

Accepting a smaller quantity than the one recorded on the invoice without a physical count. The difference surfaces later in the stocktake and is booked as shrinkage, when in fact it never entered the warehouse at all.

2. Issuing Errors

Issuing a similar item instead of the one requested, or issuing a larger quantity without recording it. Two items with near-identical part numbers are enough to produce two opposing variances in the count.

3. Unrecorded Damage

Units damaged during handling and disposed of without a documented write-off procedure.

4. Recording and Transfer Errors

Movements between locations or branches with no matching entry, or a duplicated entry.

5. Internal Theft

It exists, but it thrives precisely in environments that lack the controls above — because disorder hides the trail.

The Controls That Close Most of the Leakage

  • A mandatory physical count on receipt and a three-way match (purchase order / invoice / goods receipt).
  • Clear location coding that prevents confusion between similar items.
  • A documented write-off procedure with management approval.
  • Periodic unannounced counts of high-value items — their deterrent effect outweighs their detective effect.
  • Segregation of duties: whoever receives does not issue, and whoever issues does not adjust the balance in the system.

Start by Measuring

Establish shrinkage as a percentage of inventory value and track it monthly. The number that gets watched goes down — and the number nobody knows quietly grows.
posts.seo_title: Warehouse Shrinkage: Real Sources and Controls
posts.seo_desc: Where does warehouse shrinkage really leak? Receiving and issuing errors, unrecorded damage, transfer errors — and the controls that close most of it.

posts.title: Inventory Discrepancies: What They Really Cost You Each Year
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: The gap between physical and book stock is not just a figure in a report — it is an unnecessary purchase, a late customer order and an inaccurate set of accounts. Here we work out the real cost.
posts.body:
A Variance Is Not Just a Number in a Report

When a stocktake report shows a 3% variance between physical and book stock, many managers are inclined to treat it as an acceptable figure. But in a warehouse holding SAR 10 million of inventory, that percentage means a gap of SAR 300,000 that nobody can account for.

Three Hidden Costs That Never Appear in the Report

1. Unnecessary Purchasing

When the system shows less stock than is actually held, a purchase order is raised for an item already sitting on the shelf. Capital is tied up, storage space is consumed, and the stock is exposed to obsolescence.

2. The Late or Cancelled Order

The reverse is more dangerous: the system says the item is available, so the customer is promised a delivery date — and then the shelf turns out to be empty. The cost here is not only financial; it is customer trust.

3. Inaccurate Financial Statements

Inventory is an asset line on the balance sheet. Any flaw in its valuation feeds straight through to the financial statements and to shareholder decisions — which puts the finance function in an awkward position in front of the auditors.

Why Does a WMS Not Solve the Problem on Its Own?

A system does not correct a faulty practice — it documents it more precisely. If goods are received without a proper match, or an issue is recorded hours after the stock has physically left, the system will record the error with complete fidelity.

Where Do You Start?

Start with an independent diagnostic count that establishes the size of the gap and its sources, then fix the procedures that produced it, and finally lock in the result with a cycle counting programme that stops variances building up again.
posts.seo_title: The Real Cost of Inventory Discrepancies
posts.seo_desc: What do inventory discrepancies cost each year? Unnecessary purchasing, late orders, inaccurate accounts — and why a WMS alone won't fix accuracy.

posts.title: Annual Stocktake or Cycle Counting? When to Use Each
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: A full annual stocktake is an accounting necessity, but on its own it will not keep inventory under control all year. Here is how to combine the two intelligently without halting your operation.
posts.body:
Each Type Plays a Different Role

Confusing the annual stocktake with cycle counting leads many companies to the wrong decision: settling for a single count a year, then discovering the size of the gap once it is too late.

The Annual Wall-to-Wall Inventory

Usually carried out at the end of the financial year, it is a mandatory step in closing the books. It covers counting every item "wall to wall", and generally requires goods movement to be halted.

When is it the right choice? At financial year-end, ahead of a sale or acquisition, or when warehouse management changes.

Periodic Cycle Counting

Counting selected items at regular intervals without stopping work, usually following ABC analysis: high-value or fast-moving items are counted more often, slow movers less often.

When is it the right choice? When your operation cannot afford downtime, or when you want to catch errors early rather than waiting for year-end.

The Unannounced Control Count

A third tool that nobody serious about control can do without: counting specific items with no prior notice. Its greatest effect is deterrent rather than detective.

The Optimal Combination

One annual wall-to-wall inventory + a monthly cycle counting programme for class A items + two unannounced counts a year. This combination delivers high accuracy throughout the year with the least possible disruption to operations.
posts.seo_title: Annual Stocktake vs Cycle Counting: How to Choose

posts.title: Your Warehouse Isn't Too Small — You're Just Not Using It Well
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: Before you sign a lease on extra space, read this. In most of the warehouses we have audited, wasted space exceeded 20% — and reclaiming it was far cheaper than expanding.
posts.body:
The Most Expensive Decision Is Usually Made Too Quickly

When the warehouse fills up, the first solution that comes to mind is renting additional space. But renting adds monthly rent, more labour and movement between two sites — while the real problem usually lies in how the space is used, not in how much of it there is.

Where Does the Space Usually Disappear?

Unused Height

Many warehouses store at floor level or on low racking while the available height allows for additional levels. Cubic space is the right measure, not floor area.

Aisles Wider Than Necessary

Aisle width is dictated by the type of handling equipment. An aisle one metre wider than actually required, in a warehouse with ten aisles, means dozens of square metres wasted.

Dead Stock in the Best Locations

One of the most common things we see: items that have not moved in two years occupying the locations closest to the order preparation area, while the fast movers sit at the back.

Start with ABC Analysis

Classify your items by movement rate, then redistribute locations: class A in the nearest and most accessible locations, class C in high-level or back-of-house areas. This change alone reduces order preparation time appreciably, with no capital spend at all.
posts.seo_title: Warehouse Layout Optimisation: Reclaim Wasted Space
posts.seo_desc: Before renting more space: where does your warehouse space go? Unused height, over-wide aisles and dead stock — and how ABC analysis resets priorities.

posts.title: Five Warehouse KPIs No Operation Should Be Without
posts.author: United Integrated Team
posts.excerpt: You cannot improve what you do not measure. These five straightforward metrics can be started in any warehouse this week — and they reveal more than you would expect.
posts.body:
Why Do Most Improvement Efforts Fail?

Because they start with the solution before the measurement. Without a number before the intervention and a number after it, the discussion turns into impressions: "the work is faster now" or "things have improved" — with no evidence.

1. Inventory Accuracy

The percentage of items whose physical balance matches their book balance. It is the single most important indicator of all, and it is measured through periodic counting. Every other metric loses its meaning if this one is low.

2. Order Accuracy

The percentage of orders picked with the correct item and quantity, error-free. It measures output quality as your end customer sees it.

3. Order Cycle Time

The time from receipt of the order to despatch. It exposes bottlenecks in picking, packing and shipping.

4. Operating Cost per Square Metre

Total warehouse operating costs divided by floor area. It links operational performance directly to financial cost — and it is the metric senior management understands immediately.

5. Inventory Turnover

The number of times inventory is cleared over a given period. A decline is an early indicator of dead stock building up and capital being tied up.

Start with Just Two

Do not take on all five at once. Pick two, measure them weekly for a month, and discuss the results with the team. Discipline in measurement matters more than the number of metrics.
posts.seo_title: Five Warehouse KPIs Every Operation Needs
